claim: Metazoan IRE1 is the most evolutionarily conserved unfolded protein response (UPR) transducer.
source: Among the three signaling pathways operating in mammalian cells (IRE1, PERK and ATF6), the most evolutionarily conserved UPR transducer is IRE1, a type I transmembrane-type protein kinase and endoribonuclease (Ron and Walter, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ron and Walter, 2007

claim: When activated by ER stress, IRE1 initiates unconventional splicing of XBP1 mRNA.
source: Yeast and metazoan IRE1 activated by ER stress-induced oligomerization and trans-autophosphorylation initiates a splicing reaction and thereby specifically removes introns of 252 and 26 nucleotides from HAC1 and XBP1 precursor mRNA, respectively, which encode their respective downstream transcription factors (Mori, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mori, 2009

claim: IRE1 removes a 26-nucleotide intron from XBP1 precursor mRNA in metazoans.
source: Yeast and metazoan IRE1 activated by ER stress-induced oligomerization and trans-autophosphorylation initiates a splicing reaction and thereby specifically removes introns of 252 and 26 nucleotides from HAC1 and XBP1 precursor mRNA, respectively, which encode their respective downstream transcription factors (Mori, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mori, 2009

claim: Both unspliced and spliced XBP1 mRNA are translated in metazoan cells.
source: In contrast, because XBP1 intron is too short to block translation, both unspliced and spliced XBP1 mRNA are translated to produce the unspliced form of XBP1, designated pXBP1(U), and the spliced form of XBP1, designated pXBP1(S), in metazoan cells (Calfon et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Calfon et al., 2002 and Yoshida et al., 2001

claim: pXBP1(S) functions as a potent transcription factor.
source: Since the C-terminal region of pXBP1(S) contains a transcriptional activation domain (AD), pXBP1(S) functions as a potent transcription factor (Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2001

claim: pXBP1(U) targets pXBP1(S) to proteasomal degradation when the cell recovers from ER stress.
source: In contrast, as pXBP1(U) binds to pXBP1(S) and targets pXBP1(S) to proteasomal degradation via a domain designated degron here when the cell recovers from ER stress, pXBP1(U) functions as a negative regulator of pXBP1(S) (Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2006

claim: XBP1 precursor mRNA is expressed at a low level under normal conditions but is induced during ER stress.
source: It should be noted that XBP1 precursor mRNA is expressed at a low level under normal conditions but is induced during ER stress with a similar time course to ER chaperone mRNAs due to the presence of the same cis-acting ER stress response element in its promoter region (Yoshida et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2000

claim: pXBP1(U) suppresses autophagy by promoting the degradation of FoxO1.
source: It was also reported recently that pXBP1(U) suppresses autophagy by promoting the degradation of FoxO1 (Zhao et al., 2013) (see Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2013

claim: The adaptor molecule TRAF2 binds to activated and phosphorylated IRE1 and sequentially activates ASK1, JNKK and JNK, leading to phosphorylation and activation of c-Jun.
source: First, the adaptor molecule TRAF2 binds to activated and phosphorylated IRE1 and sequentially activates ASK1 (MEKK1), JNKK and JNK, leading to phosphorylation and activation of c-Jun (JNK pathway) (Urano et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Urano et al., 2000

claim: Activated IRE1 cleaves various mRNAs relatively non-specifically in a process called regulated IRE1-dependent decay of mRNAs (RIDD).
source: Second, activated IRE1 cleaves various mRNAs relatively non-specifically, a process called regulated IRE1-dependent decay of mRNAs (RIDD pathway) (Hollien and Weissman, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hollien and Weissman, 2006

claim: Both the JNK and RIDD pathways are pro-apoptotic.
source: Although both are pro-apoptotic (Han et al., 2009; Urano et al., 2000), the physiological significance of these two pathways remains unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2009 and Urano et al., 2000

claim: Medaka fish XBP1 mRNA has a 26-nucleotide intron that is removed in response to ER stress.
source: Here, we adopted a genetic approach toward a comprehensive understanding of IRE1 function using medaka fish (Oryzias latipes), in which removal of the 26-nucleotide intron, which is exactly the same size as that in mammals, from precursor XBP1 mRNA is observed in response to ER stress (Ishikawa et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ishikawa et al., 2011

claim: IRE1α is ubiquitously expressed and IRE1β is expressed only in the gut in mice.
source: The only difference is in the expression pattern of IRE1: although IRE1α is ubiquitously expressed and IRE1β is expressed only in the gut in mice (Bertolotti et al., 2001), both IRE1α and IRE1β are expressed ubiquitously in medaka fish (Ishikawa et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertolotti et al., 2001 and Ishikawa et al., 2011

claim: Both IRE1α and IRE1β are expressed ubiquitously in medaka fish.
source: The only difference is in the expression pattern of IRE1: although IRE1α is ubiquitously expressed and IRE1β is expressed only in the gut in mice (Bertolotti et al., 2001), both IRE1α and IRE1β are expressed ubiquitously in medaka fish (Ishikawa et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertolotti et al., 2001 and Ishikawa et al., 2011

claim: IRE1α-knockout and IRE1β-knockout medaka were generated using the TILLING method.
source: We employed the targeting-induced local lesions in genomes (TILLING) method to identify IRE1α- and IRE1β-knockout (KO) medaka, as described in Materials and methods.
evidence: Described in Materials and methods section

claim: The N-terminally truncated fragment of IRE1α (C156X) produced from the mutated allele has lost its functionality.
source: The N-terminally truncated fragment of IRE1α (C156X) or IRE1β (Y164X) produced from the mutated allele must have lost its functionality as its transmembrane, protein kinase and ribonuclease domains are excluded (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Inference based on the structure of the truncated protein shown in Figure 1B

claim: The N-terminally truncated fragment of IRE1β (Y164X) produced from the mutated allele has lost its functionality.
source: The N-terminally truncated fragment of IRE1α (C156X) or IRE1β (Y164X) produced from the mutated allele must have lost its functionality as its transmembrane, protein kinase and ribonuclease domains are excluded (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Inference based on the structure of the truncated protein shown in Figure 1C

claim: Both IRE1α- and IRE1β-single KO medaka were born and developed normally.
source: Both IRE1α- and IRE1β-single KO medaka were born and developed normally, and tunicamycin-induced splicing of XBP1 mRNA was observed normally in their embryos at 4 dpf; tunicamycin elicits ER stress by blocking protein N-glycosylation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1E

claim: Tunicamycin-induced splicing of XBP1 mRNA was observed normally in embryos of IRE1α- and IRE1β-single KO medaka at 4 dpf.
source: Both IRE1α- and IRE1β-single KO medaka were born and developed normally, and tunicamycin-induced splicing of XBP1 mRNA was observed normally in their embryos at 4 dpf; tunicamycin elicits ER stress by blocking protein N-glycosylation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1E

claim: Tunicamycin elicits ER stress by blocking protein N-glycosylation.
source: Both IRE1α- and IRE1β-single KO medaka were born and developed normally, and tunicamycin-induced splicing of XBP1 mRNA was observed normally in their embryos at 4 dpf; tunicamycin elicits ER stress by blocking protein N-glycosylation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about tunicamycin mechanism

claim: Tunicamycin-induced splicing of XBP1 mRNA was completely lost in the embryos of IRE1α/β-DKO medaka.
source: We therefore crossed the IRE1α-heterozygote with the IRE1β-heterozygote to obtain IRE1α/β-DKO medaka and found that tunicamycin-induced splicing of XBP1 mRNA was completely lost in the embryos of IRE1α/β-DKO medaka (Figure 1E).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1E

claim: IRE1α and IRE1β are redundant in medaka, unlike in mice.
source: These results indicate that IRE1α and IRE1β are redundant in medaka, unlike in mice.
evidence: Inference from the observation that single KO medaka develop normally but DKO medaka do not

claim: All IRE1α/β-DKO medaka die within 2 weeks after fertilization.
source: It should be noted that all IRE1α/β-DKO medaka die within 2 weeks after fertilization regardless of their ability or inability to hatch (data not shown here, see Figure 10A; medaka usually hatch at 7 dpf and become fertile 2 months after hatching).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 10A

claim: Complete absence of IRE1 functions is detrimental to the growth and development of medaka.
source: Thus, complete absence of IRE1 functions is detrimental to the growth and development of medaka.
evidence: Inference from the observation that IRE1α/β-DKO medaka die within 2 weeks

claim: XBP1-KO medaka were generated using the TALEN method.
source: We employed the transcription activator-like effector nuclease (TALEN) method to generate XBP1-KO medaka, as described in Materials and methods.
evidence: Described in Materials and methods section

claim: The N-terminally truncated fragment of XBP1(Δ8) produced from the mutated allele has lost its functionality.
source: The N-terminally truncated fragment of XBP1(Δ8) produced from the mutated allele must have lost its functionality as its bZIP domain is excluded (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inference based on the structure of the truncated protein shown in Figure 2A

claim: IRE1α/β-DKO medaka exhibit a short tail.
source: Close examination of embryos expressing EGFP under the control of the ER chaperone BiP promoter (PBiP-EGFPs) (Ishikawa et al., 2011) showed that both IRE1α/β-DKO and XBP1-KO medaka exhibited three defects during early embryonic development, namely a short tail (white outline in Figure 2C and D, quantification in Figure 3A) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of extracellular matrix proteins, failure of liver development (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of proteins circulating in blood, and failure of hatching gland development (red arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of hatching enzymes (proteases).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figures 2C and 3A

claim: IRE1α/β-DKO medaka exhibit failure of liver development.
source: Close examination of embryos expressing EGFP under the control of the ER chaperone BiP promoter (PBiP-EGFPs) (Ishikawa et al., 2011) showed that both IRE1α/β-DKO and XBP1-KO medaka exhibited three defects during early embryonic development, namely a short tail (white outline in Figure 2C and D, quantification in Figure 3A) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of extracellular matrix proteins, failure of liver development (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of proteins circulating in blood, and failure of hatching gland development (red arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of hatching enzymes (proteases).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 2C

claim: IRE1α/β-DKO medaka exhibit failure of hatching gland development.
source: Close examination of embryos expressing EGFP under the control of the ER chaperone BiP promoter (PBiP-EGFPs) (Ishikawa et al., 2011) showed that both IRE1α/β-DKO and XBP1-KO medaka exhibited three defects during early embryonic development, namely a short tail (white outline in Figure 2C and D, quantification in Figure 3A) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of extracellular matrix proteins, failure of liver development (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of proteins circulating in blood, and failure of hatching gland development (red arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of hatching enzymes (proteases).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 2C

claim: XBP1-KO medaka exhibit a short tail.
source: Close examination of embryos expressing EGFP under the control of the ER chaperone BiP promoter (PBiP-EGFPs) (Ishikawa et al., 2011) showed that both IRE1α/β-DKO and XBP1-KO medaka exhibited three defects during early embryonic development, namely a short tail (white outline in Figure 2C and D, quantification in Figure 3A) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of extracellular matrix proteins, failure of liver development (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of proteins circulating in blood, and failure of hatching gland development (red arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of hatching enzymes (proteases).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figures 2D and 3A

claim: XBP1-KO medaka exhibit failure of liver development.
source: Close examination of embryos expressing EGFP under the control of the ER chaperone BiP promoter (PBiP-EGFPs) (Ishikawa et al., 2011) showed that both IRE1α/β-DKO and XBP1-KO medaka exhibited three defects during early embryonic development, namely a short tail (white outline in Figure 2C and D, quantification in Figure 3A) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of extracellular matrix proteins, failure of liver development (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of proteins circulating in blood, and failure of hatching gland development (red arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of hatching enzymes (proteases).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 2D

claim: XBP1-KO medaka exhibit failure of hatching gland development.
source: Close examination of embryos expressing EGFP under the control of the ER chaperone BiP promoter (PBiP-EGFPs) (Ishikawa et al., 2011) showed that both IRE1α/β-DKO and XBP1-KO medaka exhibited three defects during early embryonic development, namely a short tail (white outline in Figure 2C and D, quantification in Figure 3A) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of extracellular matrix proteins, failure of liver development (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of proteins circulating in blood, and failure of hatching gland development (red arrowhead in Figure 2C and D) which synthesizes and secretes a large amount of hatching enzymes (proteases).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 2D

claim: The levels of Fabp10a mRNA were reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR-mediated measurements revealed that the levels of Fabp10a mRNA encoding fatty-acid-binding protein 10a, a marker of liver (Venkatachalam et al., 2009), were indeed reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos, as well as in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 3B

claim: The levels of Fabp10a mRNA were reduced to one-third in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR-mediated measurements revealed that the levels of Fabp10a mRNA encoding fatty-acid-binding protein 10a, a marker of liver (Venkatachalam et al., 2009), were indeed reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos, as well as in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 3B

claim: Fabp10a mRNA encodes fatty-acid-binding protein 10a, a marker of liver.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR-mediated measurements revealed that the levels of Fabp10a mRNA encoding fatty-acid-binding protein 10a, a marker of liver (Venkatachalam et al., 2009), were indeed reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos, as well as in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Venkatachalam et al., 2009

claim: The level of LCE mRNA was reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos.
source: Surprisingly, however, although the level of LCE mRNA encoding one of the two hatching enzymes (Yasumasu et al., 1992) was reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos, it was reduced to less than 10% in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos (Figure 3B), meaning that KO of XBP1, a transcription factor downstream of IRE1α/β, produces a much more severe phenotype than DKO of IRE1α/β in the hatching gland.
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 3B

claim: The level of LCE mRNA was reduced to less than 10% in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos.
source: Surprisingly, however, although the level of LCE mRNA encoding one of the two hatching enzymes (Yasumasu et al., 1992) was reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos, it was reduced to less than 10% in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos (Figure 3B), meaning that KO of XBP1, a transcription factor downstream of IRE1α/β, produces a much more severe phenotype than DKO of IRE1α/β in the hatching gland.
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 3B

claim: LCE mRNA encodes one of the two hatching enzymes.
source: Surprisingly, however, although the level of LCE mRNA encoding one of the two hatching enzymes (Yasumasu et al., 1992) was reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos, it was reduced to less than 10% in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos (Figure 3B), meaning that KO of XBP1, a transcription factor downstream of IRE1α/β, produces a much more severe phenotype than DKO of IRE1α/β in the hatching gland.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yasumasu et al., 1992

claim: KO of XBP1 produces a much more severe phenotype than DKO of IRE1α/β in the hatching gland.
source: Surprisingly, however, although the level of LCE mRNA encoding one of the two hatching enzymes (Yasumasu et al., 1992) was reduced to one-third in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos compared with IRE1β-single KO embryos, it was reduced to less than 10% in XBP1-KO embryos compared with WT embryos (Figure 3B), meaning that KO of XBP1, a transcription factor downstream of IRE1α/β, produces a much more severe phenotype than DKO of IRE1α/β in the hatching gland.
evidence: Inference from the observation that LCE mRNA levels are more reduced in XBP1-KO than in IRE1α/β-DKO

claim: XBP1-KO embryos could not hatch.
source: This notion was fully supported by the markedly decreased fluorescence of EGFP, which is under the control of the LCE promoter (PLCE-BiP), in the hatching gland of XBP1-KO medaka, compared with the mildly decreased fluorescence of EGFP in the hatching gland of IRE1α/β-DKO medaka (Figure 3C, D and E), and by the fact that XBP1-KO embryos could not hatch, whereas 70% of IRE1α/β-DKO embryos hatched (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 3F

claim: 70% of IRE1α/β-DKO embryos hatched.
source: This notion was fully supported by the markedly decreased fluorescence of EGFP, which is under the control of the LCE promoter (PLCE-BiP), in the hatching gland of XBP1-KO medaka, compared with the mildly decreased fluorescence of EGFP in the hatching gland of IRE1α/β-DKO medaka (Figure 3C, D and E), and by the fact that XBP1-KO embryos could not hatch, whereas 70% of IRE1α/β-DKO embryos hatched (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 3F

claim: The IRE1-XBP1 branch is required for proper development of the tail, liver and hatching gland.
source: We concluded that the IRE1-XBP1 branch is required for proper development of the three secretory organs (tail, liver and hatching gland).
evidence: Inference from the observation that IRE1α/β-DKO and XBP1-KO medaka exhibit defects in these three organs

claim: The deletion of XBP1 had no effect on the level of IRE1α mRNA.
source: The deletion of XBP1 had no effect on the level of IRE1α mRNA (Figure 5A, lanes 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, and 10), whereas the deletion of IRE1α on the background of IRE1β-KO mildly reduced the level of IRE1α mRNA (Figure 5A, lanes 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, and 12), probably due to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay of IRE1α C156X mRNA (see Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 5A

claim: The deletion of IRE1α on the background of IRE1β-KO mildly reduced the level of IRE1α mRNA, probably due to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay of IRE1α C156X mRNA.
source: The deletion of XBP1 had no effect on the level of IRE1α mRNA (Figure 5A, lanes 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, and 10), whereas the deletion of IRE1α on the background of IRE1β-KO mildly reduced the level of IRE1α mRNA (Figure 5A, lanes 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, and 12), probably due to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay of IRE1α C156X mRNA (see Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 5A, with speculation about mechanism

claim: The deletion of XBP1 markedly reduced the level of spliced XBP1 mRNA, probably due to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay of XBP1 Δ8 mRNA.
source: In contrast, the deletion of XBP1 markedly reduced the level of spliced XBP1 mRNA (Figure 5B, lanes 1, 2, 5 and 6; Figure 5C, lanes 1 and 2) as expected, probably due to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay of XBP1 Δ8 mRNA, which has the stop codon immediately after aa127 (see Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figures 5B and 5C, with speculation about mechanism

claim: The deletion of IRE1α against the background of IRE1β-KO did not significantly affect the level of spliced XBP1 mRNA at 0.5 dpf.
source: Importantly, however, the deletion of IRE1α against the background of IRE1β-KO did not significantly affect the level of spliced XBP1 mRNA at 0.5 dpf, the early gastrula stage in medaka (Figure 5C, compare lane 3 with lane 4).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 5C

claim: Maternal IRE1α WT mRNA derived from IRE1α+/− IRE1β−/− eggs was translated to produce IRE1α protein, which initiated splicing of XBP1 mRNA in IRE1α−/− IRE1β−/− (XBP1+/+) embryos at 0.5 dpf.
source: We consider that maternal IRE1α WT mRNA derived from IRE1α+/− IRE1β−/− eggs was translated to produce IRE1α (protein), which initiated splicing of XBP1 mRNA transcribed from the XBP1 locus (zygotic XBP1 mRNA), in IRE1α−/− IRE1β−/− (XBP1+/+) embryos at 0.5 dpf.
evidence: Inference from the observation that spliced XBP1 mRNA is present in IRE1α/β-DKO embryos at 0.5 dpf

claim: The presence of spliced XBP1 mRNA and thereby the presence of pXBP1(S) in embryos at 0.5 dpf stimulated development of the hatching gland at least partially in IRE1α/β-DKO medaka.
source: The presence of spliced XBP1 mRNA (Figure 5C, lane 4) and thereby the presence of pXBP1(S) in embryos at 0.5 dpf stimulated development of the hatching gland at least partially in IRE1α/β-DKO medaka.
evidence: Inference from the observation that IRE1α/β-DKO medaka have better hatching gland development than XBP1-KO medaka

claim: The hatching gland in XBP1-KO medaka developed very poorly due to the absence of spliced XBP1 mRNA and thereby the absence of pXBP1(S) in embryos at 0.5 dpf.
source: In contrast, the hatching gland in XBP1-KO medaka developed very poorly due to the absence of spliced XBP1 mRNA (Figure 5C, lane 2) and thereby the absence of pXBP1(S) in embryos at 0.5 dpf (see Discussion for more detailed explanation and Figure 10C and D for unambiguous demonstration of this maternal effect).
evidence: Inference from the observation that XBP1-KO embryos lack spliced XBP1 mRNA at 0.5 dpf

claim: Unspliced XBP1 mRNA is converted to spliced XBP1 mRNA by IRE1-mediated unconventional splicing in response to ER stress.
source: Unspliced XBP1 mRNA is converted to spliced XBP1 mRNA by IRE1-mediated unconventional splicing in response to ER stress (Figure 6B).
evidence: Established knowledge about IRE1-mediated XBP1 splicing, illustrated in Figure 6B

claim: Activated IRE1 cleaves unspliced XBP1 mRNA at two characteristic stem-7-nucleotide-loop structures.
source: Activated IRE1 thus cleaves unspliced XBP1 mRNA at two characteristic stem-7-nucleotide-loop structures as shown in Figure 6Ea.
evidence: Established knowledge about IRE1 cleavage sites, illustrated in Figure 6Ea

claim: Spliced XBP1 mRNA has lost the two stem-loop structures after the removal of the 26-nucleotide-intron.
source: Spliced XBP1 mRNA has lost such two stem-loop structures after the removal of the 26-nucleotide-intron as shown in Figure 6Eb.
evidence: Structural consequence of splicing, illustrated in Figure 6Eb

claim: Three deletions (Δ15, Δ26 and Δ4) were introduced into exon 4 containing IRE1-mediated splice sites in the XBP1 locus utilizing the TALEN and CRISPR-Cas9 methods.
source: To this end, we introduced three deletions (Δ15, Δ26 and Δ4) into exon 4 containing IRE1-mediated splice sites in the XBP1 locus (Figure 6A) utilizing the TALEN and CRISPR-Cas9 methods (Figure 6D).
evidence: Experimental procedure described in text and illustrated in Figures 6A and 6D

claim: Coexpression of medaka IRE1α markedly increased the level of medaka pXBP1(S) in the case of WT XBP1 cDNA.
source: Coexpression of medaka IRE1α markedly increased the level of medaka pXBP1(S) in the case of WT XBP1 cDNA, as expected (Figure 7A, compare lane 4 with lane 3).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figure 7A

claim: The Δ15 mutant mRNA has lost the two stem-loop structures.
source: The Δ15 mutant mRNA has lost the two stem-loop structures and that the Δ15 mutant protein lacked only five amino acids immediately C-terminal to the bZIP domain (Figure 6Ec).
evidence: Structural analysis illustrated in Figure 6Ec

claim: The Δ15 mutant protein designated pXBP1(UC) represents constitutively expressed pXBP1(U) which is not further modified in response to ER stress.
source: Thus, the Δ15 mutant protein designated pXBP1(UC) represents constitutively expressed pXBP1(U) which is not further modified in response to ER stress (Figure 6F).
evidence: Inference from the structure of the Δ15 mutant, summarized in Figure 6F

claim: The Δ26 mutant mRNA has lost 26 nucleotides which are identical to the XBP1 intron.
source: The Δ26 mutant mRNA has lost 26 nucleotides which are identical to the XBP1 intron (Figure 6D).
evidence: Structural analysis illustrated in Figure 6D

claim: The Δ26 mutant protein designated pXBP1(SC) represents constitutively expressed pXBP1(S) which is not further modified in response to ER stress.
source: Thus, the Δ26 mutant protein designated pXBP1(SC) represents constitutively expressed pXBP1(S) which is not further modified in response to ER stress (Figure 6Ed and F).
evidence: Inference from the structure of the Δ26 mutant, summarized in Figure 6F

claim: The Δ4 mutant protein is inactive due to the absence of AD, even if constitutively expressed.
source: The Δ4 mutant mRNA has lost the two stem-loop structures and the Δ4 mutant protein is inactive due to the absence of AD, even if constitutively expressed (Figure 7A, lane 11), but is switched to an active protein designated pXBP1(AS) only if removal of the entire exon 4 by alternative splicing occurs (Figure 6Ee and F).
evidence: Inference from the structure of the Δ4 mutant and experimental observation in Figure 7A

claim: Embryos in which both alleles of the XBP1 locus contained the Δ4 mutation exhibited three organ defects, similarly to XBP1-KO embryos.
source: We found that embryos, in which both alleles of the XBP1 locus contained the Δ4 mutation (Figure 8Ab), exhibited three organ defects, namely short tail (Figure 8Ea), developmental failure of the liver and hatching gland (Figure 8Fa), as well as inability to hatch (Figure 8Ga), similarly to XBP1-KO (XBP1Δ8/Δ8) embryos (Figures 2D, 3A, B and F), indicating that alternative splicing does not take place during embryonic development in medaka.
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figures 8A, 8E, 8F, and 8G

claim: Alternative splicing does not take place during embryonic development in medaka.
source: We found that embryos, in which both alleles of the XBP1 locus contained the Δ4 mutation (Figure 8Ab), exhibited three organ defects, namely short tail (Figure 8Ea), developmental failure of the liver and hatching gland (Figure 8Fa), as well as inability to hatch (Figure 8Ga), similarly to XBP1-KO (XBP1Δ8/Δ8) embryos (Figures 2D, 3A, B and F), indicating that alternative splicing does not take place during embryonic development in medaka.
evidence: Inference from the observation that Δ4/Δ4 embryos exhibit the same defects as XBP1-KO embryos

claim: XBP1UC/- embryos exhibited three organ defects, similarly to XBP1-KO embryos.
source: We found that these XBP1UC/- embryos exhibited three organ defects (Figure 8Bb), namely short tail (8Eb), developmental failure of the liver and hatching gland (Figure 8Fb), as well as inability to hatch (Figure 8Gb), similarly to XBP1-KO embryos (Figures 2D, 3A, B and F), indicating that pXBP1(U) plays little role during embryonic development in medaka.
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figures 8B, 8E, 8F, and 8G

claim: pXBP1(U) plays little role during embryonic development in medaka.
source: We found that these XBP1UC/- embryos exhibited three organ defects (Figure 8Bb), namely short tail (8Eb), developmental failure of the liver and hatching gland (Figure 8Fb), as well as inability to hatch (Figure 8Gb), similarly to XBP1-KO embryos (Figures 2D, 3A, B and F), indicating that pXBP1(U) plays little role during embryonic development in medaka.
evidence: Inference from the observation that XBP1UC/- embryos exhibit the same defects as XBP1-KO embryos

claim: The three organ defects were completely rescued in XBP1SC/- embryos.
source: Importantly, the three organ defects (Figure 8Cb) were completely rescued in XBP1SC/- embryos (Figure 8Ec,Fc) and all XBP1SC/- embryos hatched (Figure 8Gc).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by data in Figures 8C, 8E, 8F, and 8G

claim: All XBP1SC/- embryos hatched.

claim: IRE1α/β-mediated splicing of XBP1 mRNA and thus production of pXBP1(S), but not of pXBP1(U) or pXBP1(AS), is sufficient to cope with the physiological ER stress that occurs during normal growth and development of medaka fish.
source: Here, we investigated whether the JNK and RIDD pathways play critical roles in counteracting the physiological ER stress that occurred during growth and development of medaka fish. Because complete removal of the IRE1α/β genes from XBP1-KO medaka had no effect on the defects in the three organs (Figure 4), and because the defects in the three organs observed in IRE1α/β-DKO medaka were completely rescued by introduction of XBP1SC into one XBP1 allele from which fully spliced XBP1 mRNA is constitutively expressed (Figure 9), we concluded that the JNK and RIDD pathways are not required for normal growth and development of medaka fish. Thus, IRE1α/β-mediated splicing of XBP1 mRNA and thus production of pXBP1(S), but not of pXBP1(U) or pXBP1(AS), is sufficient to cope with the physiological ER stress that occurs during normal growth and development of medaka fish.
